I am not sure this is what Jeremy meant by "Yay, tests!" but, if so, I agree, unit tests can be very useful.  If it is helpful to anyone, here is a basic sketch of the approach that I included in my R and Python course last term. The approach involves three files and the testthat package.  The example that I used was a simple function to compute odds from probabilities.

myOdds v2.R:  This is the file containing my function in the working directory.
test_myOdds v2.R:  This is the file containing the unit tests for my function, in a sub-directory of the working directory called tests.
run_tests.R:  This is the file that executes the unit tests, located in the working directory.

Here is a snippet of the test_myOdds v2.R file (I am not seeing the insert code tool in the editor).  It tests that the function correctly handles three examples with scalar input.  For example a probability of .5 converts to odds of 1.  Other tests, omitted here,  focus on other kinds of input but use similar code.  Note that the file must be the source file name with the test_ prefix.

>>>
# Unit tests for myOdds.R
# Using testthat package

test_that('Scalar Values', {
  expect_equal(myOdds(.5), 1)    # P = .5 => Odds = 1
  expect_equal(myOdds(0), 0)     # P = .5 => Odds = 1
  expect_equal(myOdds(1), +Inf)  # P = 1 => Odds = +Inf
})
>>>

Here are the essential elements of the run_tests.R file that executes the tests.  The main trick here, for manual testing instead of automated testing, is to use the source() function to load the myOdds() function.

>>>
require(testthat) # testthat package

# Remember to set working directory to source of myOdds v2.R
source('myOdds v2.R', chdir=TRUE)
# identify source file of function to test
# Temporarily change working directory to source file location.

test_dir('tests')
>>>

For the version of the function that passes all the tests, the result looks like this (in the R console).  More detailed output is optionally available.

>>>
> test_dir('tests')
✓ |  OK F W S | Context
✓ |   8       | test_myOdds v2

══ Results ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
OK:       8
Failed:   0
Warnings: 0
Skipped:  0
>
>>>

I hope that is useful,
Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject_clean: How to define a latent variable by substracting two other latent variables in SEM
messages.body_plain:
Solene--
     If you want to create a model where variable c is the difference between variables a and b, you will need to create c as a dummy factor (with no variables loading on it, and then use a and b to predict c (not load on it) and give c zero residual variance. Something like this:

Model1    <- '   a =~ z1 + z2 + z3 + z4
                        b  =~ z5 + z6 + z7 + z8

                        c  =~ 0*z1
                        c ~ 1*a + -1*b
                         c ~~ 0*c '
The single ~ says that a and b predict c. The double ~~ for dependent variable c refers to c's residual variance. You might try using a different observed variable to not load on c.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input for longitudinal invariance testing
messages.subject_clean: Using polychoric covariance matrix as input for longitudinal invariance testing
messages.body_plain:
Hi, everyone.

This is my first time posting, after reading the forum posts here for a while, which I've find very helpful.

I am hoping to assess longitudinal measurement invariance for a 20-item, 2 factor scale measured at 2 timepoints. An issue I have run into is non-positive definite matrices, probably owing to small sample size (n = 109) and using categorical items with 3 response categories.

As a way to deal with NPD, I have applied smoothing algorithms to the NPD polychoric correlation matrix. My initial thinking was to use the smoothed PD matrix as input for doing the invariance testing. To do so, I converted the correlation matrix into a covariance matrix to prepare the PD matrix for use in lavaan.

Currently, my code, based on examples here and my own trouble shooting, is:

Fit.Baseline.Model <- cfa(Baseline.Model, sample.cov = poly, sample.nobs = 109, sample.mean = poly.means, estimator = "ML")

To be honest, I am guessing whether this is what should be included in the lavaan code for running longitudinal categorical CFA, since my code for the raw data is more complex than this (includes variables identified as ordered, has a parameterization command, has a different estimator selected).

Plus, I run into the following warning:

the optimizer (NLMINB) claimed the model converged, but not all
    elements of the gradient are (near) zero; the optimizer may not
    have found a local solution use check.gradient = FALSE to skip
    this check.

So, my questions for the collective wisdom here are:

What is the best way to write the cfa code for longitudinal categorical data using a polychoric covariance matrix as input? Are there any specific problems that I need to account for and how to write this in lavaan code?

With regards to the above noted warning, any guidance on dealing with this issue?

Thank you in advance,

Ian

In doing further reading, I see part of the issue I raised was covered here: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/5m2dHxCXm2A

So from this earlier conversation I see that two commands, involving user-specified matrices, are required in order to use other, more appropriate estimators (e.g., ULS, ULSMV):

WLS.V
NACOV

However, I am not certain how one goes about creating these matrices for my current context (2 time points, categorical items with 3 response options). Any guidance would be appreciated.

Further, invariance testing requires setting thresholds within the modelling syntax. Lavaan has the "sample.th <http://sample.th>" command for identifying a vector containing the sample thresholds. When I attempted to use such a vector, a warning occurred that said something about "th.idx attributes", and I was unable to find a solution to this issue.

Thanks again,

Ian

To continue the conversation (with myself, hopefully not for too much longer). In working more on this approach to using polychoric covariance matrices as input, I believe I have come up with an adequate solution.

I *believe* I am now at the point of having correctly specified all the terms/objects for the commands in CFA, and the errors I am now getting are due to the idiosyncrasies of my data, and NOT a coding error on my part.  However, given the complexity of what I am attempting and my relatively lack of confidence in using lavaan, I would be very grateful if someone with more experience can double-check how I captured thresholds, WLS.V, and NACOV for use in a CFA run. I have created a github project so anyone that has the time/will to take a look can find what I've done.

Here is the code I used to create objects that fit into the sample.cov, sample.mean, sample.th <http://sample.th>, WLS.V, and NACOV commands. You will see two separate methods to extract thresholds. The first method I do not believe actually worked when used in the CFA run, and the second method I believe did work.
https://github.com/ivmcphail/polychoric-covariances-in-lavaan/blob/main/Creating%20polychoric%20covariance%20matrix

Here is the code for the baseline model when doing longitudinal invariance testing with categorical indicators:
https://github.com/ivmcphail/polychoric-covariances-in-lavaan/blob/main/model%20syntax

And finally, here is the code, warnings, and output for the CFA run of the baseline model. I included separate runs for both methods I used to extract thresholds.
https://github.com/ivmcphail/polychoric-covariances-in-lavaan/blob/main/CFA%20run%20syntax

The warnings for the first CFA run seem to suggest this first method of extracting thresholds didn't actually do the trick. The warnings for the second CFA seem to suggest the second method for extracting thresholds did work, but that there are other problems in my data to work out. In the output, some of the thresholds look quite wild indeed.

If I am missing something in the code or if there is something else I should read/think about, I am all ears. Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Descriptive statiscs of latent variables
messages.subject_clean: Descriptive statiscs of latent variables
messages.body_plain:
The mean and standard deviation of latent variables is arbitrary, it depends on what constraints you place on the model (there are conventions that are used by almost everyone, but you don't have to use them). You can make them take on any value you want (well, as long as the SD is negative).

The standard model output gives the variance if the latent variable is exogenous, and the residual variance if it's not. It's rare to report the variance of an endogenous latent variable.

The N is the size of your sample used in the analysis. The variable is latent - unmeasured, hidden. Everyone in the sample is assumed to have a value of it.

Hope that this helps,

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Descriptive statiscs of latent variables
messages.subject_clean: Descriptive statiscs of latent variables
messages.body_plain:
As long as you are aware of the important points shared by Jeremy, if you do want to report the SDs, lavInspect(fit, what = "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") gives you the model-implied variance-covariance matrix of the latent variables. The square roots of the diagonal elements are the model implied SDs of the latent variables.

I modified the example of cfa() to create two structural models to illustrate that changing the first indicator of a factor, which by default has its loading set to one, will change the variances and SDs this factor and its covariances with other factors:

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-12
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              visual ~ textual + speed'
fit <- sem(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")
#>         visual textul speed
#> visual  0.809
#> textual 0.408  0.979
#> speed   0.262  0.173  0.384

HS.model.2 <- ' visual  =~ x3 + x2 + x1
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              visual ~ textual + speed'
fit2 <- sem(HS.model.2, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
lavInspect(fit2, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")
#>         visual textul speed
#> visual  0.431
#> textual 0.298  0.979
#> speed   0.191  0.173  0.384
```

You can remove the line 'visual ~ textual + speed' and call cfa() to see what happen to the model implied variances and covariances.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Re: How to set a specific correlation value between latent variables
messages.subject_clean: How to set a specific correlation value between latent variables
messages.body_plain:
By the default, latent variables are identified by setting the loadings of the first indicators to 1. Therefore, the variances are usually not one and we cannot constrain the correlation directly.

Assuming that it is meaningful to fix the correlation to a value, there are two ways I can think of.

We can set std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE such that exogenous latent variables are identified by constraining their variances to one. Then A ~~ .05*B constrains the correlation between A and B to .05 (assuming A and B are exogenous latent variables).

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-12
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
# Adapted from the example for cfa()
# Fix the correlation (set std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)
SE.model.2 <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              textual ~~ .05 * speed
              visual ~ textual + speed'
fit2 <- sem(SE.model.2, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)
parameterEstimates(fit2)[c(10:12, 22:24), ]
#>        lhs op     rhs   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 10 textual ~~   speed 0.050 0.000    NA     NA    0.050    0.050
#> 11  visual  ~ textual 0.468 0.093 5.016      0    0.285    0.652
#> 12  visual  ~   speed 0.417 0.102 4.105      0    0.218    0.616
#> 22  visual ~~  visual 1.000 0.000    NA     NA    1.000    1.000
#> 23 textual ~~ textual 1.000 0.000    NA     NA    1.000    1.000
#> 24   speed ~~   speed 1.000 0.000    NA     NA    1.000    1.000
standardizedSolution(fit2)[c(10:12, 22:24), ]
#>        lhs op     rhs est.std    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 10 textual ~~   speed   0.050 0.000     NA     NA    0.050    0.050
#> 11  visual  ~ textual   0.394 0.065  6.067      0    0.267    0.521
#> 12  visual  ~   speed   0.351 0.073  4.782      0    0.207    0.495
#> 22  visual ~~  visual   0.708 0.069 10.242      0    0.572    0.843
#> 23 textual ~~ textual   1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000
#> 24   speed ~~   speed   1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000
```

We can also label the variances and covariances of the latent variables, define their correlation using ":=", and constrain the correlation to a value:

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-12
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
optold <- options(width = 90)
# Adapted from the example for cfa()
SE.model.3 <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              textual ~~ vt * textual
              speed ~~ vs * speed
              textual ~~ cts * speed
              visual ~ textual + speed
              rts := cts/sqrt(vt * vs)
              rts == .05'
fit3 <- sem(SE.model.3, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
parameterEstimates(fit3)[c(10:12, 24:25), ]
#>        lhs op             rhs label   est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 10 textual ~~         textual    vt 0.974 0.112 8.720      0    0.755    1.193
#> 11   speed ~~           speed    vs 0.398 0.089 4.492      0    0.224    0.571
#> 12 textual ~~           speed   cts 0.031 0.004 7.986      0    0.023    0.039
#> 24  visual ~~          visual       0.553 0.123 4.492      0    0.312    0.794
#> 25     rts := cts/sqrt(vt*vs)   rts 0.050 0.000    NA     NA    0.050    0.050
standardizedSolution(fit3)[c(10:12, 24:25), ]
#>        lhs op             rhs label est.std    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 10 textual ~~         textual    vt   1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000
#> 11   speed ~~           speed    vs   1.000 0.000     NA     NA    1.000    1.000
#> 12 textual ~~           speed   cts   0.050 0.000     NA     NA    0.050    0.050
#> 24  visual ~~          visual         0.708 0.069 10.241      0    0.572    0.843
#> 25     rts := cts/sqrt(vt*vs)   rts   0.050 0.000     NA     NA    0.050    0.050
options(optold)
```

Both approaches involve nonlinear constraint. In my experience, convergence may fail or take a long time in some cases.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject_clean: FIML and Mean Structure
messages.body_plain:
May (or may not) be related. May I know the reason for using lavaanify() to create the parameter table, instead of letting sem() to do the job?

I also occasionally use lavaanify() myself for some purposes but using sem() and cfa() and their default options is usually a more reliable way to specify a model. If the model generated is not exactly what I want, I will override them in the model syntax. Using lavaanify() directly means that we take full responsibility on specifying the models.

I believe, if we supply the parameter table to sem() directly, it will use the table as is and so may not fix or free parameters that should be fixed or freed (please correct me if I am wrong).

You can try this and see if the parameter table generated is identical to the one you created using lavaanify() (FULL the model syntax):

tmp <- sem(FULL, missing = "fiml", do.fit = FALSE)
parameterTable(tmp)

If you need to use lavaanify() for some reasons, you can try int.ov.free = TRUE (which is FALSE by default in lavaanify()). You can check the help page of sem() to find the options it override when calling lavaanify().

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Technically, sem() does not change the model. If you give it a parameter table created by lavaanify(), it does not change it (I believe). If you give it a model syntax, then it will call lavaanify() internally, and set some of the arguments to other values so that the default values in lavaanify() are not used (e.g., int.ov.free).

It is because lavaanify() and sem() have different values for many of the options:

https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/model.syntax.html

The default of int.ov.free in lavaanify() is FALSE.

https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/sem.html

According to "Detail", the default of int.ov.free when sem() calls lavaanify is TRUE.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

P.S.: I appreciate your use of lavaanify() to make sure that the model is specified as expected. Although very convenient, the wrappers, sem() and cfa(),  sometimes do something I do not expect or may overlook if I do not read the parameter table carefully.

Sorry. I accidentally pressed "Post message" while doing cut-and-paste. The order of some sentences is strange. But I think I had better leave that post as is, rather than sending a new one with more or less the same info.

Just one clarification, in case I gave the incorrect message. sem() is a wrapper of lavaan(), not lavaanify(). But both will call lavaanify() to create a parameter table when the model is a model syntax, and will set some arguments of lavaanify() to values different from the default values of lavaanify(). That's why, with the same model syntax, the model they generate may be different from that generated by lavaanify().

-- Shu Fai

>

> https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/sem.html
>

I should be more precise:

sem() calls lavaan(), and lavaan() will call lavaanify() if necessary. So, strictly speaking, sem() set some arguments (e.g., int.ov.free = FREE) and the call lavaan(), and then these argument values will be passed to lavaanify() if it is called. sem() itself does not call lavaanify() directly.

This is how they work, as far as I understand. Please correct me if I am wrong.

messages.body_plain:
You can compare the parameter table from lavaanify and from the fitted model:

library(lavaan)

pop.FULL <- '
SOC =~  1.0 * s2 + 1.0 * s1 + 1.0 * s3 + 1.0 * s4 + 1.0 * s5 + 1.0 * s6
FIN =~  1.0 * f1 + 1.0 * f2 + 1.0 * f3 + 1.0 * f4 + 1.0 * f5 + 1.0 * f6
ETH =~  1.0 * e1 + 1.0 * e3 + 1.0 * e4 + 1.0 * e5 + 1.0 * e6
'

d <- simulateData(pop.ULL, sample.nobs = 1000)

FULL <- '

SOC =~  s2 + s1 + s3 + s4 + s5 + s6
FIN =~  f1 + f2 + f3 + f4 + f5 + f6
ETH =~  e1 + e3 + e4 + e5 + e6

'

a.FULL <- lavaanify(FULL, meanstructure = TRUE)
b.FULL <- sem(FULL, d, meanstructure = TRUE)

a.FULL[a.FULL$op == "~1",]
parTable(b.FULL)[parTable(b.FULL)$op == "~1",]

lavaanify(..., meanstrucuture = TRUE) does exactly what is explained in the documentation. Only the meanstrucuture as such is added): "meanstructure    If TRUE, intercepts/means will be added to the model both for both observed and latent variables" (https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/model.syntax.html)
model.syntax: The Lavaan Model Syntax in lavaan: Latent Variable Analysis - rdrr.io <https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/model.syntax.html>
Details. The model syntax consists of one or more formula-like expressions, each one describing a specific part of the model. The model syntax can be read from a file (using readLines), or can be specified as a literal string enclosed by single quotes as in the example below.. myModel <- ' # 1. latent variable definitions f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6 f3 =~ y7 + y8 + y9 + y10 f4 =~ y11 ...
rdrr.io <http://rdrr.io>

If you want to check if everything is parameterised the way you want it, use parTable(fit)

Best

Christian

I should be more precise:

sem() calls lavaan(), and lavaan() will call lavaanify() if necessary. So, strictly speaking, sem() set some arguments (e.g., int.ov.free = FREE) and the call lavaan(), and then these argument values will be passed to lavaanify() if it is called. sem() itself does not call lavaanify() directly.

This is how they work, as far as I understand. Please correct me if I am wrong.

-- Shu Fai

But both will call lavaanify() to create a parameter table when the model is a model syntax, and will set some arguments of lavaanify() to values different from the default values of lavaanify(). Thank you all for the help! Turns out that int.ov.free=TRUE, did the trick. Still not sure why the meanstructure=TRUE would not automatically do that, but I'll take it!

Regarding Christian's suggestion, the parameter tables from lavaanify() and the fitted model (from sem() ) were identical--neither estimated the intercepts (until int.ov.free=TRUE was set in the lavaanify()).

Cheers,

Dev

On Wed, Aug 10, 2022 at 8:16 AM Christian Arnold <Christia...@hhl.de> wrote:

> You can compare the parameter table from lavaanify and from the fitted model:
>
> library(lavaan)
>
> pop.FULL <- '
> SOC =~  1.0 * s2 + 1.0 * s1 + 1.0 * s3 + 1.0 * s4 + 1.0 * s5 + 1.0 * s6
> FIN =~  1.0 * f1 + 1.0 * f2 + 1.0 * f3 + 1.0 * f4 + 1.0 * f5 + 1.0 * f6
> ETH =~  1.0 * e1 + 1.0 * e3 + 1.0 * e4 + 1.0 * e5 + 1.0 * e6
> '
>
> d <- simulateData(pop.ULL, sample.nobs = 1000)
>
> FULL <- '
> SOC =~  s2 + s1 + s3 + s4 + s5 + s6
> FIN =~  f1 + f2 + f3 + f4 + f5 + f6
> ETH =~  e1 + e3 + e4 + e5 + e6
> '
>
> a.FULL <- lavaanify(FULL, meanstructure = TRUE)
> b.FULL <- sem(FULL, d, meanstructure = TRUE)
>
> a.FULL[a.FULL$op == "~1",]
> parTable(b.FULL)[parTable(b.FULL)$op == "~1",]
>
> lavaanify(..., meanstrucuture = TRUE) does exactly what is explained in the documentation. Only the meanstrucuture as such is added): "meanstructure    If TRUE, intercepts/means will be added to the model both for both observed and latent variables" (https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/model.syntax.html)
> model.syntax: The Lavaan Model Syntax in lavaan: Latent Variable Analysis - rdrr.io <https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/model.syntax.html>
> Details. The model syntax consists of one or more formula-like expressions, each one describing a specific part of the model. The model syntax can be read from a file (using readLines), or can be specified as a literal string enclosed by single quotes as in the example below.. myModel <- ' # 1. latent variable definitions f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6 f3 =~ y7 + y8 + y9 + y10 f4 =~ y11 ...
> rdrr.io <http://rdrr.io>
>
> If you want to check if everything is parameterised the way you want it, use parTable(fit)
>
> Best
>
> Christian
> Von: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com> im Auftrag von Shu Fai Cheung <shufai...@gmail.com>
> Gesendet: Mittwoch, 10. August 2022 13:58
> An: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
> Betreff: Re: FIML and Mean Structure
>
> I should be more precise:
>
> sem() calls lavaan(), and lavaan() will call lavaanify() if necessary. So, strictly speaking, sem() set some arguments (e.g., int.ov.free = FREE) and the call lavaan(), and then these argument values will be passed to lavaanify() if it is called. sem() itself does not call lavaanify() directly.
>
> This is how they work, as far as I understand. Please correct me if I am wrong.
>
> -- Shu Fai
>
> On Wednesday, August 10, 2022 at 7:53:39 PM UTC+8 Shu Fai Cheung wrote:
> > Sorry. I accidentally pressed "Post message" while doing cut-and-paste. The order of some sentences is strange. But I think I had better leave that post as is, rather than sending a new one with more or less the same info.
> >
> > Just one clarification, in case I gave the incorrect message. sem() is a wrapper of lavaan(), not lavaanify(). But both will call lavaanify() to create a parameter table when the model is a model syntax, and will set some arguments of lavaanify() to values different from the default values of lavaanify(). That's why, with the same model syntax, the model they generate may be different from that generated by lavaanify().
> >
> > -- Shu Fai
> >
> > On Wednesday, August 10, 2022 at 7:47:54 PM UTC+8 Shu Fai Cheung wrote:
> > > Technically, sem() does not change the model. If you give it a parameter table created by lavaanify(), it does not change it (I believe). If you give it a model syntax, then it will call lavaanify() internally, and set some of the arguments to other values so that the default values in lavaanify() are not used (e.g., int.ov.free).
> > >
> > > It is because lavaanify() and  sem() have different values for many of the options:
> > >
> > > https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/model.syntax.html
> > >
> > > The default of int.ov.free in  lavaanify() is FALSE.
> > >
> > > https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/sem.html
> > >
> > > According to "Detail", the default of  int.ov.free when sem() calls lavaanify is TRUE.
> > >
> > >
> > > Hope this helps.
> > >
> > > -- Shu Fai
> > >
> > > P.S.: I appreciate your use of lavaanify() to make sure that the model is specified as expected. Although very convenient, the wrappers, sem() and  cfa(),  sometimes do something I do not expect or may overlook if I do not read the parameter table carefully.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, August 10, 2022 at 7:11:30 PM UTC+8 dev....@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > Thank you, Shu!
> > > >
> > > > I use the lavaanify() function as an intermediary step to make sure I'm specifying the right model when the model syntax would be a little too unwieldy to write directly.
> > > >
> > > > If I'm understanding your suggestion correctly, you're suggesting that the sem() function might have different defaults than the lavaanify() parameterization causing the parameters to change again?
> > > >
> > > > I think that makes sense, but one thing I do is check the parameter table after the lavaanify() function (that is what I pasted in the post), and it shows that the intercepts are not estimated despite meanstructure=TRUE.
> > > >
> > > > The results of the sem() function support the parameter table after the lavaanify() function. I'm wondering why the lavaanify() function is not freeing the intercepts?
> > > >
> > > > Cheers,
> > > >
> > > > Dev
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Aug 9, 2022 at 9:17 PM Shu Fai Cheung <shufai...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > May (or may not) be related. May I know the reason for using  lavaanify() to create the parameter table, instead of letting  sem() to do the job?
> > > > >
> > > > > I also occasionally use lavaanify() myself for some purposes but using sem() and  cfa() and their default options is usually a more reliable way to specify a model. If the model generated is not exactly what I want, I will override them in the model syntax. Using lavaanify() directly  means that we take full responsibility on specifying the models.
> > > > >
> > > > > I believe, if we supply the parameter table to  sem() directly, it will use the table as is and so may not fix or free parameters that should be fixed or freed (please correct me if I am wrong).
> > > > >
> > > > > You can try this and see if the parameter table generated is identical to the one you created using lavaanify() (FULL the model syntax):

> > > > > parameterTable(tmp)
> > > > >
> > > > > If you need to use lavaanify() for some reasons, you can try int.ov.free = TRUE (which is FALSE by default in lavaanify()). You can check the help page of sem() to find the options it override when calling lavaanify().
> > > > >

> > > > > > > > FIML requires means in order to calculate the log-likelihood of each observation (for variables on which each person was observed).  Calculating subject i's multivariate normal density (likelihood) requires their vector of observations, the estimated mean vector, and the estimated covariance matrix.  You can see this in the  formula for the PDF <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Density_function> and by the necessity for this information in an R function (in the mvtnorm package) that calculates multivariate density:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > ?mvtnorm::dmvnorm
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Complete data does not require a mean structure because the formula for -2LL (chi-squared) can be simplified to using summary statistics (estimated using all variables from every observation).
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-pI1KVB3ou2Q/VtfyDLNXqQI/AAAAAAAAAB8/FZEi2tl7CCw/s1600/MLwithMeans.png>
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If your mean structure is saturated (or if your have mean-centered data), then the last term falls out because the difference between x-bar and mu = a vector of zeros.  When using FIML, you can't just exclude a term when your mean structure is saturated because you need to know the mean vector of the subset of variables on which that person has observed data to calculate the multivariate normal likelihood of that vector of observations.
> > > > > > > >

Le jeu. 4 août 2022 à 15:42, Edward Rigdon <edward...@gmail.com> a écrit :

> Solene--
>      If you want to create a model where variable c is the difference between variables a and b, you will need to create c as a dummy factor (with no variables loading on it, and then use a and b to predict c (not load on it) and give c zero residual variance. Something like this:
>
> Model1    <- '   a =~ z1 + z2 + z3 + z4
>                         b  =~ z5 + z6 + z7 + z8
>                         c  =~ 0*z1
>                         c ~ 1*a + -1*b
>                          c ~~ 0*c '
> The single ~ says that a and b predict c. The double ~~ for dependent variable c refers to c's residual variance. You might try using a different observed variable to not load on c.
> --Ed Rigdon
>
>

messages.body_plain:
That's rather not the case. Maybe you are using a different version of lavaan. Watch out for the highlighted typo, maybe that was the reason:

library(lavaan)

pop.FULL <- '
SOC =~  1.0 * s2 + 1.0 * s1 + 1.0 * s3 + 1.0 * s4 + 1.0 * s5 + 1.0 * s6
FIN =~  1.0 * f1 + 1.0 * f2 + 1.0 * f3 + 1.0 * f4 + 1.0 * f5 + 1.0 * f6
ETH =~  1.0 * e1 + 1.0 * e3 + 1.0 * e4 + 1.0 * e5 + 1.0 * e6
'

d <- simulateData(pop.FULL, sample.nobs = 1000)

FULL <- '
SOC =~  s2 + s1 + s3 + s4 + s5 + s6
FIN =~  f1 + f2 + f3 + f4 + f5 + f6
ETH =~  e1 + e3 + e4 + e5 + e6
'

a.FULL <- lavaanify(FULL, meanstructure = TRUE)
b.FULL <- sem(FULL, d, meanstructure = TRUE)

a.FULL[a.FULL$op == "~1",]
parTable(b.FULL)[parTable(b.FULL)$op == "~1",]

pe <- parameterEstimates(b.FULL)
pe[pe$op == "~1",]

The script produces the expected results (nevertheless, I completely agree with you that the behavior of lavaanify is not intuitive - Best Christian):

> > > > > > > > FIML requires means in order to calculate the log-likelihood of each observation (for variables on which each person was observed).  Calculating subject i's multivariate normal density (likelihood) requires their vector of observations, the estimated mean vector, and the estimated covariance matrix.  You can see this in the  formula for the PDF <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Density_function> and by the necessity for this information in an R function (in the mvtnorm package) that calculates multivariate density:
> > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Complete data does not require a mean structure because the formula for -2LL (chi-squared) can be simplified to using summary statistics (estimated using all variables from every observation).

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If your mean structure is saturated (or if your have mean-centered data), then the last term falls out because the difference between x-bar and mu = a vector of zeros.  When using FIML, you can't just exclude a term when your mean structure is saturated because you need to know the mean vector of the subset of variables on which that person has observed data to calculate the multivariate normal likelihood of that vector of observations.

messages.body_plain:
That's a fun solution Ed!

Another approach would be to residualize as per latent difference score/latent change score models:

a ~ 1*b
a ~~ 0*a
c =~ 1*a

Here, c is what's left after differencing with b, because  a ~ 1*b is the same as a - b, which is the basis for all the latent difference score/latent change score models.

If anyone is interested, in my upcoming Longitudinal SEM seminar in R, I'm covering a similar approach in the cross-lagged panel model case. Check it out at Instats now -- it's filling up fast though, so get in quick!

https://instats.com/workshop_info/1651738159709x220035937550467070

Best wishes
Mike

messages.subject: AW: how to do convergent and discriminant validity check in R？
messages.subject_clean: AW: how to do convergent and discriminant validity check in R？
messages.body_plain:
Hello Min,

here is a quick and dirty written function for simple one-group CFA that produces the "usual" result. If desired, HTMT is inserted in the upper triangular matrix.

No guarantee that everything is correct - please check the results!

Note: Discriminant validity is a strange phenomenon. One can argue about it forever. In any case, it makes sense to read Rönkkö/Cho (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1094428120968614) and consider their advice.

Best

Christian

library(lavaan)
library(semTools)

# Creates the "usual" table
rel <- function(object, CR = TRUE, AVE = TRUE, MSV = TRUE, HTMT = TRUE, digits) {
  cor.lv <http://cor.lv> <- data.frame(lavaan::lavInspect(object, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>"))
  pt <- lavaan::parTable(object)[lavaan::parTable(object)$op == "=~",]
  mtrx <- round(cor.lv <http://cor.lv>, digits)
  diag(mtrx) <- ""
  if(HTMT) {
    htmt  <- round(semTools::htmt(paste(pt[,"lhs"], pt[,"op"], pt[,"rhs"], sep = ""), data.frame(lavaan::lavInspect(object, "data"))), digits)
    upper <- htmt[upper.tri(htmt)]
  }
  else upper <- ""
  mtrx[upper.tri(mtrx)] <- upper
  if(MSV) mtrx <- cbind(MSV = round(sapply(abs(cor.lv <http://cor.lv>), function(x) max(x[x != max(x)])^2), digits), mtrx)
  if(AVE) mtrx <- cbind(AVE = round(semTools::AVE(object), digits), mtrx)
  if(CR)  mtrx <- cbind(CR = round(semTools::compRelSEM(object), digits), mtrx)
  return(mtrx)
}

# Example
pop.model <- "
f1 =~ 1.0 * x1 + 1.0 * x2 + 1.0 * x3
f2 =~ 1.0 * x4 + 1.0 * x5 + 1.0 * x6
f3 =~ 1.0 * x7 + 1.0 * x8 + 1.0 * x9
f1 ~~ 0.4 * f2
f1 ~~ -0.3 * f3
f2 ~~ -0.6 * f3
"

model <- "
f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9
"

set.seed(1)
data <-  simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 1000)

fit <- cfa(model, data)

rel(fit, CR = TRUE, AVE = TRUE, MSV = TRUE, HTMT = TRUE, digits = 3)

messages.body_plain:
Let me elaborate a little on Mikko's answer (Mikko, congrats on the article).  First, of course, 'convergent validity' and 'discriminant validity' are terms that are out of step with the modern understanding of validity.  These are not distinct and independent types of validity that one collects like stamps in a stamp collection (Guion's analogy).  Instead, they are lines of evidence that contribute to a unified validity argument for your measure(s).  This is related to the idea that validation is not like going through a checklist of independent steps.  As such, it is best to avoid thinking of validation in terms of "checking" and instead think of it as an evaluation or assessment of validity involving inter-related lines of evidence.

The lasting contribution of Campbell and Fisk's article that seems to get lost is that they recognized and attempted to solve the "how big is big" problem.  There are no universal cut scores for how related measures of the same construct should be or how unrelated measures of different constructs should be.  This depends on the constructs.  (Moreover, shifting attention to the items instead of the measures asks a very different question and should not be treated simply as a matter of expedience.)  As Zumbo and Chan have emphasized, Campbell and Fisk focused on the comparative sizes of the above associations, suggesting that associations between measures of different constructs set a lower bound for associations between measures of the same construct, and conversely, associations between measures of the same construct set an upper bound for associations between measures of different constructs.  These are just outer-bounds; depending on your constructs, you might want to set the bar lower for discrimination and higher for convergence.  The fundamental point is that the two need to be evaluated in relation to one another, not separately.

More generally, no statistical analysis offers a gold standard or operational definition of convergence of measures of the same construct or discrimination of different construct by different measures.  (This relates back to the checklist idea.)  Any one analysis is just one line of evidence for these hypotheses.  Ideally, a program of research should triangulate on these hypotheses using different lines of evidence.  At the very least, no one analysis should ever be interpreted as offering definitive evidence.  When you report your results, remember that they are only partial and that they are fallible.  Interpret the results in light of all the evidence available to help you critically evaluate your measures.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Error with invariance testing
messages.subject_clean: Error with invariance testing
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am having some trouble sorting out an error I am getting when performing measurement invariance testing. I am using measEQ.syntax in semTools and the problem arises when I try to incorporate complex survey design characteristics using lavaan.survey. Here's the code I ran:

model <- '
latent =~ v1 + v2 + v3 + v4 + v5 + v6
v1 ~~ v6
v5 ~~ v6
'

baseline <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = model,
                              data = data,
                              ordered = c("v1", "v2", "v3", "v4",
                                          "v5", "v6"),
                              parameterization = "delta",
                              ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>",
                              ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                              group = "group",
                              group.equal = "configural")

model_baseline <- as.character(baseline)

fit_baseline <- cfa(model = model_baseline, data = data, group = "group", ordered = c("v1", "v2", "v3", "v4", "v5", "v6"))

This code works and summary(fit_baseline) provides error free results. But the error occurs when I try to account for the survey design:

survey_weight <- svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~strata, weights = ~weight, data = data, nest = TRUE)

fit_baseline_surv <- lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit = fit_baseline, survey.design = survey_weight, estimator = "DWLS")

Error in start[th.idx] <- th.values[match(th.names.lavpartable, th.names.sample)] :
  replacement has length zero

Any ideas about how I could fix this issue?

Thanks for your help,
Micah

messages.subject: Re: Changing the estimator
messages.subject_clean: Changing the estimator
messages.body_plain:
The value we use in the argument "estimator" is a shortcut to a set of options. You can refer to the following post:

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/6oLwoboi-vQ/m/IQLAXChPAwAJ

So, the estimator did not really change to "DWLS". WLSMV represents a set of options, DWSL being one of them.

(Note that the table is not official nor final, there may be other things that need to be considered but I forgot to include them.)

You can also read this excellent paper on those options (and more):

https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10705511.2021.1877548

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject: Interactions between auto.efa and other arguments
messages.subject_clean: Interactions between auto.efa and other arguments
messages.body_plain:
Could someone explain how the `auto.efa` argument interacts with other arguments in lavaan? This argument is TRUE by default in lavaan::cfa() but there are other arguments that seem able to conflict with this and the documentation does not note the priority system.

Documentation describes auto.efa as follows:

"auto.efa: If TRUE, the necessary constraints are imposed to make the (unrotated) exploratory factor analysis blocks identifiable: for each block, factor variances are set to 1, factor covariances are constrained to be zero, and factor loadings are constrained to follow an echelon pattern."

Meawhile, auto.var is described as:

"auto.var: If TRUE, the residual variances and the variances of exogenous latent variables are included in the model and set free."

Within cfa(), these are both set to TRUE. However, if auto.var frees the variances of exogenous latent variables and auto.efa is supposed to constrain them to 1, it's not clear what this default is (supposed to be) doing.

Perhaps I am misunderstand what an "exploratory factor analysis block" is defined as in this case, but I do not see documentation on this either.

messages.subject_clean: Obtaining unstandardized factor scores in CFA
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm trying to extract factor scores from a CFA to use in further analysis. The model is a
longitudinal measurement invariance model with one factor and two measurement points. I'm using the empirical bayes modal since the individual items are ordinal (and ML yields some unplausible data, likely due to skewness of item distributions).

 In further analysis I want to test for several latent mean changes between the measurement points in the context of a cross lagged panel model using the intercepts of the second measurement points. Hence the question -  is it possible to get unstandardized factor scores of the latents with lavPredict using EBM?

The model was estimated using DWLS and strong MI is enforced (thresholds + loadings constrained) - if that is of any help.

Thanks a lot!

Best
Alex

messages.subject: Re: interpret/rescale lavPredict scores
messages.subject_clean: interpret/rescale lavPredict scores
messages.body_plain:
The common factor has no scale of measurement, and its scale along the real-number line is arbitrarily assigned.   If your binary indicator is based on the observed response scale, then it is a function of a composite from the indicators, not a function of a common factor in a CFA model.

If you are willing to make more restrictive assumptions (e.g., parallel measurement, equality of thresholds across items), then you could use SEM to specify a generalizability-theory model, which would allow you to evaluate the dependability (absolute reliability) of a composite using a designated cutoff score.

https://doi.org/10.3390/psych3020011

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Multi-group comparison for RI-CLPM
messages.subject_clean: Multi-group comparison for RI-CLPM
messages.body_plain:
> we also would also like to see if the groups differ in their random intercepts for each variable (mean levels of each variable over time).

Do you mean testing whether the average random-intercept (latent mean) differs across groups?  Measurement invariance is imposed by virtue of equal loadings across groups (all loadings are 1, to give the latent intercept its interpretation).  But the latent means are fixed to zero for identification.  I think in this case you could hypothetically use effects-coding constraints on the intercepts over time to estimate the random intercept's mean.  The problem is that the first occasion's intercept doesn't have the same interpretation as the remaining occasions' intercepts, because you aren't regressing the first occasion on a previous occasion.

What I would recommend instead is labelling all of your intercepts (unique labels across groups), then defining group-difference parameters, which will have delta-method SEs and tests in your summary() output.  You can use lavTestWald() to obtain a single omnibus test statistic that all 5 group differences == 0, and the individual tests on each occasion would be follow-up tests if the omnibus H0 is rejected.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> Is that reasonable to conduct chi-squared difference test on them?

No, the models are not nested.  To test the null hypothesis that there is no cluster-level variance to model, you can fit your single-level model as the Level-1 component of a MLSEM, whose Level-2 component simply fixes all (co)variances to zero.  That model is nested in the MLSEM in which the Level-2 parameters are estimated, so you can conduct a chi-squared difference test.

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

It should not be necessary to use rawData=; just specify your population parameters explicitly in the lavaan syntax or the SimSim model objects.  Then the population parameters you specify will be available in the SimResult object, so summaryParam() will be able to automatically calculate bias, etc.

FYI, to use variable sample sizes across replications in a multigroup setting, you need to pass a list of integer-vectors to n=.  Each list element corresponds to 1 group, and each integer in the group's vector represents the sample size of that group in replication [i].  Thus, each list element needs the same length().  So for 5 replications of 3 groups, each with a random N between 50 and 100, it would look like this.

set.seed(123)
ngroups <- 3
nReps <- 5
MyNs <- lapply(1:ngroups, function(g) sample(50:100, size = nReps))

[[1]]
[1] 80 64 63 52 91

[[2]]
[1] 99 92 86 63 74

[[3]]
[1] 75 76 54 99 77

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Adding covariates causes bad model fit
messages.subject_clean: Adding covariates causes bad model fit
messages.body_plain:
When you add time-invariant covariates, you have expanded the mean vector and covariance matrix that the model is trying to reproduce.  If the covariates only predict the growth factors, then they can only indirectly affect the observed indicators of growth, which limits the way they can contribute to the model-implied means and covariances.  If they can directly affect the growth indicators instead, and their effects vary over time, that implies the covariate's effect is moderated by time, which is a more complex model.  They should be nested, so you can compare fit to test the H0 of no moderation by time.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I'm conducting a multilevel path analysis by using Lavaan and I have the outcome variables as residuals of T1 (sqa_interest) and T2 (sqb_pint) variables (e.g., interest). model1 <- lm(sqb_pint ~ sqa_interest, data=mydata, na.action = na.exclude)

(output the residuals for level 1 and level 2 separately) I would have to slightly adjust the syntax for the models, using the level-specific residuals (for level 1 the residuals of level 1 and for level 2 the residuals of level 2). An example syntax for the model is below.
Model_direct_cog <- '
    level: 1
    standard_res_interest2 ~ sqa_cog
     level: 2
    standard_res_interest2 (?) ~ sqa_cog
             '

summary(fitModel_direct_cog, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

Thanks a lot and I appreciate your help!
Aysenur

messages.subject: RI-CLPM - Time-invariant standardized lagged effects - lavaan ERROR: unknown label(s) in variable definition(s): a c b d
messages.subject_clean: RI-CLPM - Time-invariant standardized lagged effects - lavaan ERROR: unknown label(s) in variable definition(s): a c b d
messages.body_plain:
Hello there,

I want to model my data with a Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel model according to Moulder's & Hamaker's website <https://jeroendmulder.github.io/RI-CLPM/lavaan.html#The_RI-CLPM>.
The basic model produces no error. However, for complexity reduction, I want to constrain the model for "Time-invariant standardized lagged effects" (syntax by clicking on the folder after "The RI-CLPM") produces the following error message:

Error in lav_partable_constraints_def(partable, con = LIST, debug = debug) :
  lavaan ERROR: unknown label(s) in variable definition(s): a c b d

However, I had to do some adaptations to my model syntax, because unlike Moulder's & Hamaker's syntax, I have only four measurement time points (my syntax is below and data is attached).
My adaptation procedure was such that I deleted any line that referred to a variable at t5.

The error message refers probably to the lower two batches of code, in which " correlations of within-components" are computed and " residual variances of within-components" are constrained.
In there, the ":=" operator ought to define additional parameters (a, b, c, d), but this does not work, as the error message tells.
Maybe one needs fewer additional parameters for four time points?

I would be very happy for any thoughts about this :)

best regards,
Korbinian

My adapted syntax is as follows:
RICLPM <- '
  # Create within-components with freely estimated factor loading
  wx1 =~ NA*x1
  wx2 =~ NA*x2
  wx3 =~ NA*x3
  wx4 =~ NA*x4
  wy1 =~ NA*x1
  wy2 =~ NA*x2
  wy3 =~ NA*x3
  wy4 =~ NA*x4

  # Set variances of within-components at first wave to 1
  wx1 ~~ 1*wx1
  wy1 ~~ 1*wy1

  # Estimate correlation between within-components at first wave
  wx1 ~~ cor1*wy1

    # Label the residual covariances
  wx2 ~~ rcov2*wy2
  wx3 ~~ rcov3*wy3
  wx4 ~~ rcov4*wy4

  # Label the residual variances
  wx2 ~~ rvx2*wx2
  wy2 ~~ rvy2*wy2
  wx3 ~~ rvx3*wx3
  wy3 ~~ rvy3*wy3
  wx4 ~~ rvx4*wx4
  wy4 ~~ rvy4*wy4

    # Compute correlations of within-components at each wave
  cor2 := a*c + b*d + a*d*cor1 + b*c*cor1 + rcov2
  cor3 := a*c + b*d + a*d*cor2 + b*c*cor2 + rcov3

  #! Contrain residual variances of within-components such that variance of each within-component equals 1
  rvx2 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor1)
  rvy2 == 1 - (c*c + d*d + 2*c*d*cor1)
  rvx3 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor2)
  rvy3 == 1 - (c*c + d*d + 2*c*d*cor2)
  rvx4 == 1 - (a*a + b*b + 2*a*b*cor3)
  rvy4 == 1 - (c*c + d*d + 2*c*d*cor3)
'
RICLPM.fit <- lavaan(RICLPM, data = ep_pr, missing = 'ML', meanstructure = T, int.ov.free = T)
summary(RICLPM.fit, standardized = T)

Hi Rémi
Thank you for posting this. An ideal use case would be automatically calculating total effects from early to later occasions in cross-lagged panel models. In econometrics these are called impulse responses, but with many occasions of measurement over time T, the 'by hand' calculations of all indirect effects becomes very unwieldy. Mplus makes this easy with the IND command, but lavaan does not. This would be an ideal use case for automated total effect calculations in lavaan as the sum of all indirect effects from early to later occasions across all AR and CL paths in cross-lagged panel models.

In case it's helpful, you can read about impulse responses in cross-lagged panel models in the following:

Zyphur, M. J., Allison, P. D., Tay, L., Voelkle, M. C., Preacher, K. J., Zhang, Z., ... & Diener, E. (2020). From data to causes I: Building a general cross-lagged panel model (GCLM). Organizational Research Methods, 23(4), 651-687.

Shamsollahi, A., Zyphur, M. J., & Ozkok, O. (2022). Long-run effects in dynamic systems: New tools for cross-lagged panel models. Organizational Research Methods, 25(3), 435-458.

Best wishes
Mike

Korbinian,
I encounter the same error in my head when reading your code as Lavaan does.  When I get to the first constraint, I can find definitions of cor1 and rcov2 in the previous code, but I cannot find any prior reference to a, b, c and d.  I am completely out on a limb here, but there are 4 parameters and the form of the calculation looks like what one would obtain by calculating the correlation between two items in a two-factor factor analysis (sum of products of loadings on the same factor plus sums of products of loadings on different factors times the factor correlation).  If that is what you are doing, then you need to add the a-d labels to the fist block of code.  According to the model.syntax help file, you cannot use syntax like a*NA*x1 but instead need to use syntax like a*x1 + NA*x1 where 'a' is a label and 'NA' indicates a free parameter.  Caveat:  I am not seeing the use of 'NA' in the sample code that you pointed to.  I imagine that you are overriding constraints imposed by some convenience function but I am not crystal clear on what you are up to with those.  So, do not take this post as vetting your code.

I hope that helps,
Keith

messages.subject: Re: Interactions between auto.efa and other arguments
messages.subject_clean: Interactions between auto.efa and other arguments
messages.body_plain:
The auto.efa argument only applies to 'efa' blocks. In that case, they
override all other arguments (including auto.var) that would conflict
with this.

Consider this syntax:

model <- '
     # efa block
     efa("efa1")*f1 +
     efa("efa1")*f2 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6

     # cfa block
     f3 =~ y7 + y8 + y9
     f4 =~ y10 + y11 + y12

     # regressions
     f3 ~ f1 + f2
     f4 ~ f3
'

The efa() left-hand modifier is used to define an 'explorary' block of
latent variables, which implies they will be rotated.

In the same model, we can still have regular/unrotated 'cfa' blocks. For
those blocks, the auto.var argument still applies.

Yves.

On 8/18/22 23:12, Robert Wilcom wrote:
> Could someone explain how the `auto.efa` argument interacts with other
> arguments in lavaan? This argument is TRUE by default in lavaan::cfa()
> but there are other arguments that seem able to conflict with this and
> the documentation does not note the priority system.
>

> *Documentation describes auto.efa as follows:*

>
> "auto.efa: If TRUE, the necessary constraints are imposed to make the
> (unrotated) exploratory factor analysis blocks identifiable: for each
> block, factor variances are set to 1, factor covariances are constrained
> to be zero, and factor loadings are constrained to follow an echelon
> pattern."
>

> *Meawhile, auto.var is described as:*

>
> "auto.var: If TRUE, the residual variances and the variances of
> exogenous latent variables are included in the model and set free."

> *
> *
> *Within cfa(), these are both set to TRUE. However, if auto.var frees

> the variances of exogenous latent variables and auto.efa is supposed to
> constrain them to 1, it's not clear what this default is (supposed to

> be) doing.*
> *
> *
> *Perhaps I am misunderstand what an "exploratory factor analysis block"
> is defined as in this case, but I do not see documentation on this either.*
>

Hi Korbinian and Keith,

I just happen to stumble on this question while searching for something else, and might as well help out. The labels a b c d refer to the lagged effects (see the "Constraints over time" tab). So I made a mistake in saying " Compared to the basic model (...)"; it should say "Compared to the previous model (with constraints over time on the unstandardized effects) (...)". I have just changed this on the website, and added a complete model syntax for the RI-CLPM with constraints on the standardized effects. I hope this is useful. Please let me know (via j.d.m...@uu.nl) if you still encounter problems here.

Jeroen

When I get to the first constraint, I can find definitions of cor1 and rcov2 in the previous code, but I cannot find any prior reference to a, b, c and d. If that is what you are doing, then you need to add the a-d labels to the fist block of code.  According to the model.syntax help file, you cannot use syntax like a*NA*x1 but instead need to use syntax like a*x1 + NA*x1 where 'a' is a label and 'NA' indicates a free parameter. I imagine that you are overriding constraints imposed by some convenience function but I am not crystal clear on what you are up to with those.  So, do not take this post as vetting your code.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I've developed a package for doing power analyses for the RI-CLPM. It is based on Monte Carlo simulations. Now, my focus is on speeding up the power analysis. Do you have suggestions for how to decrease the time it takes for lavaan to estimate models? I've have already implemented the following features:
Parallel processing across different simulation conditions (for different number of sample sizes, number of time points, etc.).
Use the population parameter values as starting values for estimating the model.
Suggestions are greatly appreciated.

All the best,
Jeroen

messages.subject: Re: Options to speed up repeated analyses using lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Options to speed up repeated analyses using lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jeroen,

If you need to fit the same model over and over again using different
(simulated) datasets, then I would recommend to use the lavaan()
function in combination with the slot* arguments. For example, if the
model does not change, you may be able to keep the Model slot (if
fixed.x = FALSE), the parameter table, etc.

In addition, you can 'switch off' a number of actions that you don't
need (for example baseline = FALSE, h1 = FALSE, implied = FALSE,
post.check = FALSE, ...).

Have a look at how things are implemented in lavaanList(), or
lav_bootstrap_internal() (although in both cases there is much room for
improvement).

Yves.

If all you want to do is extract the residual variance of observed indicators, you can just use:

or

Hi Jasper,
Thanks so much for the reply. I believe you are very close, because theta is indeed the parameter I am interested in. My only concern is that this function returns me a single value, the estimate,  for each indicator. I am wondering if maybe I can get estimates for each observation used - Just as I did for the factor scores.

See this mention in Kim et al., 2021's Publication on Internalizing Dimensions and All-Cause Mortality :

"To model the transdiagnostic internalizing factor, we used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), including four indicators (MDD, GAD, panic disorder, and neuroticism) assessed at MIDUS 1. After modeling internalizing, we saved the factor scores to include them in the main Cox regression model."
"In order to compare the predictive validity of internalizing versus disorder‐unique variance, we parameterized an explicit residual variance factor for each of the three internalizing disorders and neuroticism (i.e., the unique variance remaining in each indicator after the common variance is accounted for by the latent internalizing variable). We then saved the factor scores from transdiagnostic internalizing and the four construct residual factors, and regressed survival time on both internalizing and the residual factor scores simultaneously."

This is what I am trying to accomplish. Just as I used that for loop that gives me factor score estimates for each observation, I wish to do the same with residual variances for use in regression with an outside variable. Perhaps I can insert your suggested function in my for loop? Let me know your thoughts.

-Zach
